explanation: Double-quoted strings process escape sequences and variable interpolation, while single-quoted strings are treated as almost literal.
The ?? operator checks with isset() semantics, so undefined variables or array keys yield null instead of emitting a warning.
The echo construct accepts multiple arguments separated by commas and outputs them concatenated, so 'a' and 'b' are printed together as 'ab'.
print is an expression in PHP that returns the value 1, so it can be embedded inside larger expressions like assignments.
The ?: operator returns its left operand when it is truthy and its right operand when the left operand is falsy.
In PHP 8, the . operator has the same precedence as + and - and they are left-associative, so 1 . 2 + 3 evaluates as (1 . 2) + 3 = 15.
The ** operator is right-associative in PHP, so 2 ** 3 ** 2 evaluates as 2 ** (3 ** 2) = 2 ** 9 = 512.
In PHP 8 the concatenation operator has lower precedence than +, so it evaluates as 'sum: ' . (2 + 3).
Strict comparison (===) requires arrays to have the same key/value pairs in the same order with the same types, so element order matters.
0 == false is a loose comparison that returns true, not false.
In PHP 8, comparing a non-numeric string with an integer converts the number to a string, so "abc" == 0 evaluates to false (it was true only in PHP 7 and earlier).
In PHP, null is loosely equal to 0, "", and false, so all three comparisons evaluate to true.
PHP converts the leading numeric portion of the string to an integer, stopping at the first non-numeric character.
PHP converts the numeric string '5' to an integer and performs numeric addition.
In PHP, casting false to string yields an empty string "", while casting true yields "1" and casting 0 yields "0".
Floating-point representation causes 0.1 + 0.2 to equal 0.30000000000000004, so strict equality with 0.3 fails.
strrev() operates on bytes, so it can split multibyte UTF-8 characters and produce invalid output.
str_contains() returns true when the needle 'world' is found within the string 'Hello world'.
str_pad() can pad on the left (STR_PAD_LEFT), right (STR_PAD_RIGHT), or both sides (STR_PAD_BOTH).
By default trim() strips spaces along with \n, \r, \t, \v and \0, so tabs and newlines are removed too.
strlen counts bytes, and 'é' is 2 bytes in UTF-8, so 1+2+1+1+1 = 6.
A negative start position counts from the end, so substr returns the last 3 characters.
ucfirst() returns a new capitalized string and does not modify the original in place, since PHP strings are immutable value types.
Heredoc (<<<EOT) interpolates variables and escape sequences, while nowdoc (<<<'EOT') treats its contents as a literal string with no interpolation.
sort() reindexes the array and only preserves values, whereas functions like asort() preserve key-to-value associations.
PHP automatically casts valid decimal integer strings (like '5') used as array keys to integers.
in_array() uses loose comparison (==) by default; strict comparison only occurs when the third argument $strict is set to true.
Without a callback, array_filter() removes all elements that are considered falsy (empty strings, 0, null, false, etc.).
By default array_slice() reindexes numeric keys unless the preserve_keys parameter is set to true.
array_slice() extracts 2 elements starting at index 1, giving 20 and 30.
The union operator keeps the left-hand value for duplicate key 'a' and adds 'b' from the right array, giving 2 elements.

PHP 8.1 added support for spreading arrays with string keys in array literals, merging string-keyed arrays like [...$a, ...$b] without preserving duplicates of string keys (later keys override earlier ones).
They can be combined as long as the unpacked arguments appear before the named ones (e.g. foo(...$args, c: 3)); only unpacking after named arguments is disallowed.
Anonymous functions create their own scope and must use the `use` keyword to inherit variables from the outer scope.
func_num_args() returns the number of arguments passed to the function, which is 3.
In PHP, an arrow function (fn) body must be a single expression; it cannot be enclosed in curly braces with multiple expressions, which would be a regular function.
PHP arrow functions capture their free variables by value at the moment the arrow function is created, not lazily by reference when it is called.
A static closure has no $this binding, so it cannot access the current object context.
The closure captures $x by value at definition time, so it returns 5 even after $x is reassigned to 7.
Without strict_types, PHP coerces the numeric string "5" to int, so the call is allowed.
PHP 8.0 introduced constructor property promotion, so `public function __construct(private int $x) {}` declares and assigns a private property in one step.
The final keyword applied to a method prevents it from being overridden in any subclass.
A final method prevents any subclass from overriding it, so the statement is true.
Private members are only accessible within the class that defines them, so a subclass cannot access a parent's private properties.
Anonymous classes are named "class@anonymous" followed by a NUL byte and then the declaring file path plus line number.
Private parent methods are invisible to the child, so a child can redefine the same name with any visibility without a compatibility error.
__get() is invoked when accessing either a non-existent property or an inaccessible (private/protected) property, so it is not limited to non-existent ones.
In PHP, modifying (reassigning) a readonly property throws an Error (e.g., 'Cannot modify readonly property'), not an Exception, since it is a fatal engine-level violation.
PHP interfaces may declare constants, which implementing classes inherit.
The instanceof operator returns true if the given object is an instance of the specified class or implements the specified interface.
PHP interfaces may declare static methods, and implementing classes must provide their own static implementations.
The instanceof operator checks both class inheritance and interface implementation.
PHP interface methods are implicitly public and abstract and cannot contain a body; only traits provide default method implementations.
Abstract methods can be declared as public, protected, or private, so protected visibility is valid for an abstract method in an abstract class.
Foo::cases() returns an array containing all defined cases, which are A, B, and C, for a total of 3 elements.
Since PHP 8.2, traits may declare constants, which are then available in any class using the trait.
In PHP 7+, the Throwable interface is implemented by both Exception and Error, making it their common ancestor.
TypeError extends Error rather than Exception, so a catch (Exception $e) block will not catch it.
The @ operator only suppresses error messages (warnings, notices, etc.), not exceptions, which must be handled with try/catch.
intdiv() with a zero divisor throws DivisionByZeroError, unlike the fdiv() function which returns INF.
The finally block runs whether or not an exception is caught, and executes even if no exception occurs at all.
An exception thrown in a finally block overrides the try block's result by propagating and discarding any pending return or exception.
Casting any object to bool yields true in PHP, since all objects are considered truthy.
Calling exit triggers PHP's shutdown sequence, which runs functions registered with register_shutdown_function().
A use statement only creates an alias for namespace resolution; the class file is loaded lazily when the class is first referenced (e.g., instantiated).
In PHP, the `use function` statement is used to import functions from namespaces, while `use const` is used for constants.
The PSR-4 mapping strips the App\ prefix and appends .php, giving src/Controller/Api/UserController.php.
Composer's generated autoloader uses spl_autoload_register() to register its class-loading functions when vendor/autoload.php is included.
The magic constant __NAMESPACE__ resolves to the name of the current namespace as a string, or an empty string if the code is outside any namespace.
An unqualified class name is resolved relative to the current namespace; only a leading backslash resolves from the global root.
PSR-4 strips the prefix App\ and appends the remaining relative path Model\User to src/, yielding src/Model/User.php.
The `use` import statement must appear in the outermost scope of a file or inside a namespace declaration; placing it in a function body is a compile-time fatal error.
PHP arrays use value semantics with copy-on-write, so assigning one array variable to another copies the array rather than creating a reference.
Arrays are assigned by copy in PHP, so modifying $b does not affect $a, which still has 2 elements.
PHP functions have their own local scope, so global variables require the global keyword, $GLOBALS array, or parameter passing to access.
unset($GLOBALS['x']) removes the variable globally, since $GLOBALS is a reference to the actual global symbol table.
inc() takes $n by reference and increments it, so $n becomes 6.
foreach by value iterates over a copy of the array (copy-on-write), so modifications inside the loop do not affect the ongoing iteration, whereas foreach by reference does operate on the live array.
A static property belongs to the class itself and is shared among all instances, so changes are visible everywhere.
PHP converts boolean array keys to integers (true becomes 1 and false becomes 0), so they are stored as int, not bool.
Since PHP 7.0, generators can return a value, which can be retrieved with $gen->getReturn() after the generator has finished.
Once a generator has run to completion, calling rewind() throws an exception ("Cannot rewind a generator that was already run").
yield from delegates iteration to another generator or iterable, forwarding values and messages between them.
g() returns a Generator instance, and get_class returns the class name as a string.
The generator yields three values from [1, 2, 3], so iterator_to_array returns an array with 3 elements.
SplStack implements a LIFO (last-in, first-out) stack, while SplQueue implements a FIFO queue.
ArrayIterator implements the Iterator interface, allowing an array to be traversed with foreach and other iterator methods.
ArrayObject implements IteratorAggregate, so it can be traversed with foreach.
Since PHP 5.5, password_hash() automatically generates a cryptographically random salt, and passing a custom salt explicitly is deprecated in modern PHP.
In PHP 8, PASSWORD_DEFAULT is bcrypt (PASSWORD_BCRYPT), which uses the $2y$ algorithm, not md5.
password_verify compares 'secret' against its hash and returns true since they match.
strip_tags() only removes HTML/PHP tags; SQL injection must be prevented with prepared statements or proper escaping.
session_regenerate_id() creates a new session ID, preventing an attacker's pre-set session ID from being reused after login.
php_sapi_name() returns the SAPI module name, such as 'cli' for command-line.
session_destroy() only removes server-side session data; the session cookie must be deleted separately using setcookie().
You must call session_start() first to initialize the session and populate $_SESSION with stored session data.
The array_find() function, along with array_find_key(), array_any(), and array_all(), was added in PHP 8.4.
Property hooks were introduced as part of PHP 8.4, allowing get and set logic to be defined directly in the property declaration.
PHP 8.4 introduced asymmetric visibility, allowing a property to be publicly readable but restricted for writing with constructs like private(set).
The #[\NoDiscard] attribute was introduced in PHP 8.5 to warn when a function's return value is intentionally ignored.
The pipe operator |> was accepted via RFC and introduced in PHP 8.5.
The clone-with syntax clone($obj, ['x' => 1]) has never been introduced in any PHP version; cloning with modified properties still requires implementing the __clone() method.
PHP has no array_first() or array_last() functions; only array_key_first() and array_key_last(), added in PHP 7.3.
The Partial Function Application v2 RFC was accepted during PHP 8.6's development cycle, i.e. targeted at PHP 8.6 (current as of 2026-11-07).
The clamp_v2 RFC adding the clamp() function was targeted at and implemented for PHP 8.6, which was the version in development as of 2026-11-07.
PHP has no adopted Context Managers RFC; context-manager-style resource handling is still done manually with try/finally or dedicated classes, so the claim is false.
There is no such accepted or declined PHP RFC titled 'Bound-Erased Generic Types', so the claim is false.
No RFC making ZTS (thread-safe) builds the PHP default has been accepted, so PHP still ships NTS as the default configuration.
PHP still lacks native generics support; they are only emulated via tools like Psalm and PHPStan annotations as of PHP 8.5.
PHP releases yearly, so 8.5 (Nov 2025) remains the latest stable until 8.6's GA on 2026-11-19, after the 2026-11-07 date.
Development of PHP 6 (planned Unicode support) was abandoned, so the version numbering jumped from 5.6 to 7.0.
The RFC was accepted and the #[\Deprecated] attribute was added to PHP 8.4 core.
In clean and onion architecture, dependencies always point inward, so inner (domain) layers never reference outer layers like infrastructure or UI.
Domain entities should depend only on the language and standard library to keep the domain layer framework-agnostic and testable.
Controllers and Twig templates belong to the presentation (interface) layer, since the business-logic layer is where the use cases themselves reside.
In onion architecture, the innermost layer is the domain model/entities containing core business rules, surrounded by successively outer layers.
Tools like deptrac analyze layer dependencies and fail the build when a forbidden call between layers is detected.
In clean architecture, a use case should depend only on abstract ports and simple input DTOs, not on framework-specific objects like an HTTP request or an EntityManager.
A Repository provides collection-like access to aggregates while hiding the underlying persistence mechanism behind an interface.
The database is an infrastructure concern in the outer layer, so domain entities and use cases depend only on abstractions like repository interfaces.
An aggregate is a cluster of domain objects treated as a consistency boundary, not necessarily mapped to a database table.
In Domain-Driven Design, Value Objects are immutable and equality is determined by their attribute values rather than object identity.
In Domain-Driven Design, the aggregate root is the only object external code may use to modify the aggregate's internal state.
In Domain-Driven Design, repositories manage aggregate roots as consistency boundaries, while internal entities are accessed only through their root.
Ubiquitous language is the shared, consistent language used by both developers and domain experts in Domain-Driven Design.

In Domain-Driven Design, a bounded context is the boundary within which a domain model and its ubiquitous language stay consistent, while outside it the same terms may denote different models/meanings in other contexts.
DDD favors a rich domain model where behavior and business logic live in domain objects, making the anemic model an anti-pattern.

In Domain-Driven Design, a bounded context defines a boundary within which a domain model is consistent and unified, so the same concept (e.g., 'Customer' or 'Order') in different contexts is modeled as a distinct class with its own attributes, rules, and invariants.
Symfony services are instantiated only when they are first fetched from the container, not when the container is built.
The 'debug:router' command (previously 'router:debug') lists all routes registered in a Symfony application.
Autowiring automatically discovers and wires services based on type hints, so manual declarations are typically unnecessary.
Twig compiles each template into a PHP class and caches the compiled file to avoid recompilation on subsequent requests.
Symfony compares the timestamps of the files tracked as container resources on each request and only recompiles the container when one of them changed.
The APP_ENV environment variable determines the active Symfony environment (e.g. dev or prod).
Symfony can only invoke public methods on a controller, so a private method cannot be routed to.
Event subscribers are not given inherent priority — their ordering depends on the priority set when registered, just like listeners.
Symfony 5.1 introduced the new authenticator-based security system, and the legacy Guard authenticators were removed in Symfony 6.0, leaving AuthenticatorInterface as the standard approach.
The IsGranted attribute from Symfony Security denies access with a 403 unless the given role/permission is granted to the current user.
Symfony's security voters evaluate attributes like 'EDIT' against a specific object (e.g., a post) via the AccessDecisionManager when calling isGranted().
Symfony 7 removed doctrine/annotations support, so validation constraints must be declared as PHP 8 attributes.
Symfony enables CSRF protection on forms by default and validates the token during form submission.
Symfony always re-validates submitted data on the server during form handling, regardless of any browser-side HTML5 validation.
The Symfony MakerBundle command `php bin/console make:form` generates a new FormType class.
Symfony stores only the user's identifier and roles in the session, never the plain-text password, which is only verified during authentication.
In Symfony, application-level bundle/config options are stored as YAML files in config/packages, conventionally one file per bundle or topic (e.g., framework.yaml, doctrine.yaml).
It is a common convention to commit a .env file containing development defaults while keeping real secrets in .env.local, which is excluded via .gitignore.
The debug:container command lists all registered services and their aliases in the dependency injection container.
Parameters are inlined into the compiled service definitions at build time, so changing them at runtime has no effect on already-created services.
Since Symfony 4, services are private by default and must be explicitly marked as public to be fetched directly from the container.
Bundles typically ship with sensible default configuration, so a config file in config/packages is optional and not required for a bundle to work.
Symfony's dependency injection container supports %env(VAR)% placeholders in services.yaml that are resolved at runtime from environment variables.
The APP_DEBUG environment variable controls whether Symfony runs in debug mode, enabling the profiler and Twig debugging.
A single message can be handled by multiple handlers; all of them receive the message when it's dispatched.
The sync transport handles messages immediately in the same process rather than queueing them for a worker.
The `bin/console messenger:consume` command starts the worker that processes queued Messenger messages.
In Symfony's Messenger component, retry_strategy (including max_retries, delay, multiplier, etc.) is defined under each transport's configuration in config/packages/messenger.yaml.
Symfony Messenger's default serializer is PhpSerializer, which uses native serialize()/unserialize(), while the JsonSerializer must be configured explicitly.
The Symfony Scheduler component generates recurring messages according to configured triggers and dispatches them through the Messenger component for handling.
The Doctrine Messenger transport persists messages in database tables using Doctrine DBAL.
Symfony Messenger buses allow registering custom middleware with 'before' and 'after' options relative to the built-in ones.
Symfony releases a major version (X.0) every two years in November and minor versions every six months in May and November.
Symfony 8.0 requires PHP 8.4 or higher as its minimum supported PHP version.
Symfony 7.0 removed support for docblock annotations, requiring PHP attributes instead, which replaced annotations since 6.x.
Symfony's AssetMapper component serves and bundles CSS/JS assets directly by mapping PHP-imported paths through an importmap, removing the need for Node.js or Webpack.
Symfony 6.4 is an LTS (Long-Term Support) release, providing three years of maintenance and bug fix support.
Symfony removes code that was deprecated in the previous major branch when the new major version is released (e.g. 4.0 removed what was deprecated in 3.x).
Symfony provides UPGRADE-*.md files (e.g., UPGRADE-4.0.md, UPGRADE-5.0.md) in its repository that document all breaking changes for each major version.
The AssetMapper component lets you manage assets and the importmap without needing Node.js or Webpack.
Symfony minor releases arrive near the end of May and November, so 8.2 would not come out until around November 30, 2026, after 2026-11-07.
Symfony follows a six-month minor release cycle, so after 8.1 in May 2026, 8.2 would be due in November 2026.
Symfony follows a May/November release cycle, so after 8.1 (November 2026) comes 8.2 in May 2027.
8.2 is a minor version, not a major release, and Symfony follows a deprecation policy so apps aren't fully rewritten.
PHP follows semantic versioning, so minor releases within a major branch maintain backward compatibility and should not require code changes.
Symfony 8.4 (November 2027) is the final minor/LTS release of the 8.x branch, coming just before the 9.0 major release.
Symfony only raises its minimum PHP version in major releases, so Symfony 8.2 would still require PHP 8.4 as set by 8.0.
Following Symfony's BC policy, code deprecated in the 8.x branch is only removed in the next major release, i.e., Symfony 9.0.
Twig only allows its own filters, functions, and template logic, never arbitrary PHP code.
Twig's autoescaping feature is enabled by default for the html strategy, so printed variables are HTML-escaped unless explicitly disabled.
The |e (escape) filter in Twig escapes a string for safe output, defaulting to the HTML context.
The twig/intl-extra bundle provides the format_number filter (based on Intl NumberFormatter) to format a number according to a locale.
The Twig |raw filter marks a value as safe so auto-escaping is skipped when it is printed.
In Twig, {{ }} outputs an expression's value while {% %} handles control structures like if, for, and set.
Twig allows declaring variables inside templates using the {% set %} tag, in addition to receiving values from the controller.
Twig's dump() function outputs the debug structure of a variable, similar to PHP's var_dump().
Bootstrap is a front-end CSS/JS toolkit for styling UI components, whereas SPA frameworks (like Angular, Vue, React) handle application logic and routing.
The .container class sets a responsive fixed max-width that changes at each Bootstrap breakpoint, unlike .container-fluid which is always 100% wide.
Bootstrap's grid is based on floats (in classic versions) but is split into 12 columns, not 16.
Bootstrap 5 defines the named breakpoints sm, md, lg, xl, and xxl, giving five infixes for responsive classes.
In Bootstrap, spacing utilities like .mt-3 and .px-2 are generated from the $spacer variable, where the number represents a multiplier of that base spacing value.
Bootstrap 5 uses the data-bs-toggle attribute (e.g. data-bs-toggle="dropdown") to activate interactive components.
Bootstrap 5 removed its jQuery dependency and components are implemented using vanilla JavaScript.
Bootstrap 5.3 enables dark mode via the data-bs-theme="dark" attribute on the root element, not a .dark class.
Doctrine requires explicit schema tool operations like doctrine:schema:create or migrations; it does not auto-create tables when an entity is first used.
EntityManager::persist() schedules a new entity for insertion, making it managed, but no SQL is executed until flush() is called.
EntityManager::merge() was removed in Doctrine ORM 3.0, so it no longer exists.
DQL is an object-oriented query language that operates on entity classes and their fields, abstracting away the underlying database tables and columns.
The find() method returns null when no record matching the given primary key is found.
Doctrine does not automatically flush changes; you must call flush() manually on the EntityManager to persist changes.
A managed entity is already tracked by the Unit of Work, so flush() performs dirty-checking and issues an UPDATE automatically; persist() is only needed to register a new/transient entity.
In Doctrine, remove() only schedules the entity for deletion; the SQL DELETE statement is generated and executed when flush() is called.
MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) allows readers and writers to operate concurrently without blocking each other, since readers see a snapshot of data from when their transaction began.
The EXPLAIN command displays a query's execution plan without actually running it.

SERIAL is a PostgreSQL shorthand that creates a sequence and sets a default, whereas GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY is the SQL-standard mechanism with stricter behavior (e.g., preventing direct updates and managing its own sequence), so they are not the same thing.
By default PostgreSQL's UNIQUE constraint treats NULLs as distinct, allowing multiple rows with NULL; only PG15+ offers the NULLS NOT DISTINCT option to change this.
string_agg(value, delimiter) is the PostgreSQL aggregate function that concatenates strings into one, separated by the given delimiter.
Plain VACUUM only reclaims dead tuple space for reuse within the table; only VACUUM FULL (which rewrites the table) returns that space to the operating system.
In a window function, the PARTITION BY clause divides the result set into groups over which the window function is computed.
READ COMMITTED prevents dirty reads but still allows non-repeatable reads, since each statement sees the latest committed data and values may change between reads within a transaction.
PostgreSQL runs in autocommit mode by default, so each statement not already in an explicit transaction block is committed automatically as its own implicit transaction.
COMMIT finalizes the current transaction, permanently saving all changes made within it.
Indexes speed up finding rows for WHERE clauses, so UPDATE and DELETE statements that filter on an indexed column also benefit.
PostgreSQL supports the SQL standard SAVEPOINT statement, which lets you roll back to a specific point within a transaction, undoing only the statements executed after it.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query and reports both the plan and real execution statistics (timing, rows), unlike plain EXPLAIN which only shows the plan without executing.
pgvector is a PostgreSQL extension that adds the vector data type and supports exact and approximate nearest-neighbor search indexes for embeddings.
A partial index only indexes rows matching the WHERE condition, making it smaller and faster for queries that fit the predicate.
PostgreSQL implements SERIALIZABLE using Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) with predicate locking on data in-flight, not by locking rows that transactions read.
HTTP status 201 'Created' indicates that the request was successful and resulted in the creation of a new resource.
204 No Content indicates success with no body, commonly returned after DELETE requests.
The HTTP specification classifies DELETE as idempotent because repeating the request leaves the resource in the same state (removed), even if later responses return 404.
The Access-Control-Allow-Origin header is sent by the server, not the client, to indicate which origins are permitted to access the resource.
HTTP status 429 Too Many Requests is specifically defined for when a user has sent too many requests in a given amount of time (rate limiting).
4xx codes indicate client-side errors, while 5xx codes indicate server-side errors, so the statement has them reversed.
The Content-Type header specifies the media type (MIME type) of the request or response body.
RFC 5789 explicitly states that PATCH is not required to be idempotent, whereas PUT must be.
Plain == is a loose comparison vulnerable to PHP type juggling (e.g. '0e...' magic hashes) and timing attacks, so hash_equals() should be used instead.
A synchronizer token is generated per session by the server and checked on the server side before processing unsafe state-changing requests.
The Content-Security-Policy HTTP response header enables and configures the CSP policy for the document.

OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework, not an authentication protocol; the access token grants access to resources rather than proving user identity (for that you need something like OpenID Connect).
XSS is primarily prevented by escaping/encoding output when rendering it in the browser, not merely by validating input before storing it.
The authorization code is returned via the redirect_uri query parameter and then exchanged for an access token at the token endpoint.
Refresh tokens have a longer lifespan than access tokens and are used to obtain new access tokens without requiring re-authentication.
Salts are stored alongside the hash (usually in the database) and only need to be unique, not secret, since verification just needs the salt plus the hash.
PHPUnit only runs tests in classes that extend PHPUnit\Framework\TestCase.
setUp() runs before each individual test method, while setUpBeforeClass() runs only once before all tests in the class.
A data provider supplies multiple sets of arguments, running the test once per set.
PHPUnit's expectException() declares that an exception of the given class is expected to be thrown.
It's the reverse: in PHPUnit, mocks are configured with expectations and verify which methods were called, while stubs simply return canned data.
PHPUnit 10 deprecated doc-comment annotations like @dataProvider in favor of PHP 8 attributes such as #[DataProvider].
PHPUnit requires tests to be independent and self-contained, so relying on another test's result is not supported.
The --random-order option tells PHPUnit to execute tests in a randomly shuffled order.
